passages.text: Trial Analysis and Interpretation in Critical Care Using the Evidential (Likelihood) Approach: Rationale and Practical Considerations

Selecting the optimal methodological framework for evidence synthesis presents a fundamental challenge in contemporary clinical research. In critical care, in which many interventions yield inconclusive results under traditional P value–based analyses, complementary analytical approaches can enhance our understanding of trial data. Although frequentist statistics remain predominant and Bayesian methods have recently experienced a resurgence of interest, the evidential (or likelihood) framework offers a methodological perspective that potentially bridges these two inferential paradigms. In this Concise Translational Review, we introduce readers to the evidential approach. To present the evidential approach as an analytical tool for critical care trials, we demonstrate its application using data from two mechanical ventilation trials (ART [the Alveolar Recruitment Trial], N = 1,010; and STAMINA [Strategy for Community Acquired Pneumonia Trial], N = 214) and one trial evaluating balanced solutions (BaSICS [Balanced Solutions in Intensive Care Study], N = 10,520). We focus on how concepts and terminology translate across paradigms, the framework’s measures of effect (i.e., likelihood ratios, support values, and support intervals), proposals for its use in sequential analysis and trial monitoring, and how to report results from this framework in research articles. We propose that the evidential framework provides a clinically intuitive approach to trial interpretation by focusing on the relative evidence between competing hypotheses, thereby offering additional and complementary insights that align with clinical reasoning processes. To facilitate implementation by the scientific community, we have developed an interactive Shiny (open-source web-based) application (https://fzampier.shinyapps.io/Likelihood_Shiny/).

The frequentist paradigm remains predominant in critical care research. Although its core strength lies in controlling error rates in inference, researchers and clinicians have persistently noted conceptual challenges in directly translating P values and confidence intervals into clinical decision-making. These challenges have motivated the exploration of alternative and complementary analytical approaches that may better align with clinical reasoning in certain contexts. Among these statistical frameworks, the evidential framework warrants consideration as a bridge between frequentist objectivity and the growing appeal of the interpretability offered by Bayesian statistical thinking. In what follows, we use the term “evidential approach” interchangeably with the “likelihood approach” and opt for the former terminology whenever both are applicable, reflecting its growing prominence in recent literature. This manuscript introduces how likelihood-based evidence metrics can refine clinical inference and potentially recalibrate decision thresholds in critical care practice using examples from recent clinical trials.
A Summary of Frequentist and Bayesian Thinking

The frequentist approach based on null hypothesis testing under a Neyman-Pearson framework remains the most dominant method used by researchers in biomedical research. Recently, there has been a resurgence in the use of Bayesian methods, with critical care at the vanguard. This revived interest has been driven by conceptual and empirical limitations of the frequentist approach, which many clinicians perceive as suboptimal for translating data analysis into clinical care. More specifically, frequentists interpret probability as the long-term objective frequency of events; that is, the proportion of times an event would occur if an experiment were repeated indefinitely under identical conditions. Frequentist hypothesis testing involves calculating and interpreting P values. The P value provides a probability on a continuum of observing data as extreme or more extreme than what was observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true, with decisions made by comparing it versus a prespecified significance level (α), typically 0.05. Frequentists do not assign probabilities to hypotheses themselves, only to data under hypotheses. Hence, frequentist analyses provide the probability of data under a hypothesis (P[data | hypothesis]), in which clinicians are seldom actually interested.

Bayesian inference enables clinicians to obtain the probability of a hypothesis given their data and a prior belief (that is, P[hypothesis | data, prior]). The available data (i.e., the likelihood) are combined with the prior belief to provide posterior probabilities for inference. Hence, the Bayesian understanding of probability is not tied to long-term frequencies but to the degree of belief. For instance, rather than stating: “Given the null hypothesis is true, results as or more extreme as the one observed would occur 5% of the time,” a Bayesian analysis might conclude: “There is an 85% probability that this treatment reduces mortality,” which is intuitively a more useful declaration.

Nonetheless, Bayesian methods have peculiarities that some interpret as shortcomings. Although priors are expected to reflect the available knowledge at the time the test is conducted, there is tension regarding how priors should be set. Specifically, concerns exist that priors can be adjusted to favor a given hypothesis, introducing the unwelcome specter of bias when reporting Bayesian analyses. Further, the presentation of Bayesian results using multiple different priors can appear elusive, making it challenging to convince expert clinicians and scientists steeped in a frequentist paradigm. Finally, most reporting guidelines emphasize frequentist analyses, and many regulatory agencies continue to require them, occasionally permitting Bayesian analyses if they also account for events, such as type I error rate, that are not inherent to Bayesian reasoning.
The Likelihood as a Bridging Concept

The likelihood functionally estimates how well an explanation fits the observed data. Frequentists use the likelihood concept for likelihood ratio (LR) tests to compare how well two hypotheses or models explain the data. Bayesians use likelihood to obtain posteriors by blending them with priors. There is a fundamental connection between evidential and frequentist approaches, as both assess compatibility between data and hypotheses. However, whereas frequentist methods typically focus on the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what was observed under a null hypothesis (P value), the evidential approach directly compares how compatible the data are with competing hypotheses without reference to hypothetical repeated sampling. Therefore, it is also possible, and often informative, to use likelihoods independently to assess evidence. This evidential approach compares the compatibility of different hypotheses with the data without relying on long-term frequentist frequencies or Bayesian priors (Figure 1 and Table 1). It is important to note that, when Bayesian analyses employ minimally informative priors, the resulting posterior distribution closely approximates the normalized likelihood function, yielding numerically similar results. However, the evidential approach maintains a distinct philosophical stance by focusing solely on the relative compatibility of data with different hypotheses without making probabilistic claims about the hypotheses themselves. This approach can enhance trial interpretation, and clinical readers are likely quite familiar with the concept of likelihood (Table 2). Specifically, the LR is a fundamental concept in diagnostic test interpretation. An LR of a specific value (X) for a diagnostic test indicates that the observed test results are X times more likely to occur in patients with the disease than in those without it. This framework naturally extends to the evaluation of comparative hypotheses after data collection, providing an evidential summary of the relative compatibility of observed results with the effect sizes of interest.

A comparison of the frequentist (panel A), evidential (panel B), and Bayesian (panel C) approaches for a simulated trial with two trial arms, each consisting of 30 patients. The intervention has a mean outcome value of 35, whereas the control has a mean of 30, with standard deviations of 10. In panel A, the frequentist approach compares the results (thick black line) with the null effect, i.e., the probability of observing values as extreme or more extreme than those found when the null hypothesis is true (two-tailed P value) is indicated in the darkest areas, and the confidence intervals (CIs) are displayed. The analysis concludes that the mean estimated effect is +5.71, with a 95% CI ranging from 0.06 to 11.36. In panel C, a Bayesian analysis of the same results is depicted using a neutral normal prior (centered at the mean difference of 0 and with a standard deviation of 2.5), represented by the light gray dotted line. The data, i.e., likelihood, are shown on the solid line. The posterior arises from combining the prior and the likelihood using Bayes’s theorem, resulting in the posterior distribution (dashed gray line). The results are expressed as a mean difference of +2.5 with 95% credible intervals ranging from −1.16 to 6.18, which is more conservative than the frequentist approach given the neutral prior. The analysis also provides the probability of a positive effect (0.91) and the probability of a large effect (greater than 3, around 0.40). Further queries of interest could have been obtained. Finally, the evidential approach is illustrated in panel B, showing how it provides a bridge between these two popular frameworks. The relative likelihood of values for the difference between groups is shown for specific values delimited by brackets. Note how the likelihood ratio (LR) is simply the ratio of the heights for y values in the likelihood function. Therefore, there is moderate support (S) for a difference of 5 versus null (LR of 7.5, S of 2.01) and virtually no support for the comparison between a difference of 8 versus 3 (LR of 1.14, S of 0.13). Values from 0.1 to 11.3 are well supported by the data. Note how the evidential approach does not provide absolute probabilities for specific values, but relative likelihood when comparing two values. It is also independent of a null distribution (unlike a frequentist analysis) and does not require a prior definition. Note how the curve for the data is always represented as a solid black line and is similar in both approaches.

Although various thresholds have been proposed, there is no universally accepted standard equivalent to P < 0.05 in frequentist statistics. Commonly referenced guidelines from Goodman suggest interpreting S values as: 1–2, weak evidence; 2–3, moderate evidence; 3–4, strong evidence; and >4, very strong evidence. These correspond to LRs of approximately 2.7–7.4 (weak), 7.4–20.1 (moderate), 20.1–54.6 (strong), and >54.6 (very strong evidence). Unlike P value thresholds, these are interpretive guidelines rather than strict decision boundaries.
Key Concepts on the Evidential Approach

ConceptDefinition
Law of the likelihoodThe fundamental principle stating that observed data support one hypothesis over another proportionally to the ratio of their likelihoods. This principle forms the theoretical foundation of the evidential approach to statistical inference.
Likelihood functionA function that indicates how well various potential treatment effects correspond with observed data. It measures the compatibility between observed trial results and potential effect sizes. The peak of this function represents the effect size that best fits the data (MLE).
Likelihood ratioThe ratio of likelihoods for two different parameter values indicates how much more compatible the data is with one effect size compared with another. For example, an LR of 8 between two points indicates that the data are eight times more compatible with one effect size than the other. It is simply the ratio of heights from the likelihood function.
SupportThe natural logarithm of the LR, which simplifies interpretation by transforming the multiplicative scale to an additive one. Support values exceeding 2 are typically regarded as moderate evidence (like P < 0.05 in traditional statistics). According to Goodman, S values between 1 and 2 indicate weak evidence, between 2 and 3 moderate evidence, between 3 and 4 strong evidence, and >4 very strong evidence.
S−2 and S−3 intervalsRanges of parameter values reasonably compatible with observed data. The S−2 interval encompasses all parameter values where comparison with the MLE yields support no less than −2 (LR no less than 0.135 or 1/7.4). The S−3 interval is broader, including values with support no less than −3 (LR no less than 1/20) when compared with the MLE. These intervals are conceptually similar to confidence intervals but focus on compatibility with data rather than long-term frequencies.
MLEThe parameter value at the peak of the likelihood function that best explains the observed data. It represents the most compatible effect size given the trial results from a statistical model.

A Brief Introduction to Evidential Analysis (and Some Technical Details)

The likelihood function indicates how well various possible treatment effects correspond with the observed data; that is, it is a measure of compatibility. Consider a curve in which the x-axis represents different possible treatment effects, such as differences in mortality or days requiring ventilation in Figure 1, and the y-axis shows how closely each potential effect aligns with our observed data. The peak point on this curve signifies the effect size that best fits our data: this is the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE).

Yet, the power of likelihood analysis lies in comparing different points on this curve. We achieve this using LRs. An LR of 8 between two points indicates that the data are eight times more compatible with one effect size than the other. In the hypothetical trial illustrated in Figure 1 (see online supplement for code), the LR for a treatment effect of 5 units compared with no effect (zero) is 7.5. This means that a treatment effect of 5 is 7.5 times more likely than no effect, given our data. We can calculate these ratios between any two points on the curve, not just in comparison with the absence of effect. The LR will equal the Bayes factor for simple point-versus-point analysis (see online supplement).

To aid in interpretation, LRs are often presented on a logarithmic scale as support (S). The benefits include changing the range from −infinite to +infinite and the additive properties of logarithms, i.e., the logarithm of a product equals the sum of the logarithms of the factors (log[x × y] = log[x] + log[y]). Support values exceeding 2 are typically regarded as moderate evidence, similar to how P < 0.05 denotes significance in frequentist statistics. Interpretation is nuanced, with increasing S values indicating greater support for one hypothesis over another. According to Goodman and Royall, S values between 1 and 2 are considered weak evidence, values between 2 and 3 moderate evidence, values between 3 and 4 strong evidence, and values greater than 4 very strong evidence. Like confidence intervals, likelihood or support intervals exist. The S−2 support interval encompasses parameter values consistent with the MLE, meaning that, when any value within it is compared with the MLE, it will yield an S of no less than −2. This also signifies that comparing any two parameter values within the interval will produce an S within the range from −2 to +2. Support plots can also be created (see below). Further technical details on S intervals and their comparison with confidence intervals and Bayesian high-density posterior intervals are discussed in technical note 2 in the data supplement.
Why We Like the Likelihood Analysis for Clinical Research

What we find attractive about likelihood analysis is that, when we have built the likelihood function, we can ask any question about the relative support for different effect sizes without penalty or consideration of priors. By “without penalty,” we mean that LRs and S values retain their interpretation regardless of how many comparisons are made or how many times the data are examined, unlike P values, which require adjustment for multiple testing. However, it is essential to note that, even when likelihood-based results are used with prespecified decision thresholds (e.g., those in formal stopping rules), the risk of erroneous conclusions remains, as it does in any statistical framework. The distinction is that the evidential approach offers flexibility in assessing exploratory evidence without altering the mathematical interpretation of the ratios themselves. For instance, we might compare the likelihood of a clinically meaningful benefit versus harm. In terms of traditional diagnostic test metrics, a positive LR equals sensitivity/(1 − specificity), whereas a negative LR equals (1 − sensitivity)/specificity. This interpretive framework naturally extends to the evaluation of comparative hypotheses after data collection, providing an evidential summary that quantifies the relative compatibility of observed results with the effect sizes of interest. Thus, just as a positive test result might be “10 times more likely in patients with the disease than without,” evidential analysis allows us to assert that a treatment effect of “X is 10 times more likely than Y” based on our data.
Practical Examples Using the ART, STAMINA, and BaSICS Trials
Background on the Trials

ART (the Alveolar Recruitment Trial) and the STAMINA (Strategy for Community Acquired Pneumonia) trial were designed to evaluate whether optimizing positive end-expiratory pressures (PEEP) could improve outcomes for patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). ART employed a recruitment maneuver followed by a PEEP titration strategy, whereas STAMINA used a PEEP titration method based on respiratory system compliance, but with less aggressive recruitment and a greater emphasis on maintaining low driving pressures. Both trials adopted the ARDSNet low PEEP/FiO2 table in the control group. Whereas ART included patients with ARDS of any cause, STAMINA specifically focused on patients with community-acquired pneumonia. ART enrolled 1,010 patients with the primary endpoint of 28-day mortality. Results indicated a higher mortality rate (55.3% vs. 49.3%; P = 0.041) and fewer ventilator-free days (VFDs; 5.3 vs. 6.4 d; P = 0.03) in the intervention group. STAMINA aimed to enroll 500 patients to evaluate VFD at 28 days as the primary endpoint but was halted after 214 patients as a result of site fatigue and funding issues. The mean VFD was 6 days in the intervention group compared with 7 days in the control group (P = 0.28). Both trials suggested potential harm from the intervention. BaSICS (the Balanced Solutions in Intensive Care Study) was a large (N = 10,520) pragmatic clinical trial comparing balanced solutions versus 0.9% saline solution for unselected critically ill patients, with 90-day mortality as the primary endpoint (26.4% in the balanced solution arm vs. 27.2% in the saline arm; P = 0.47).
Reanalyzing with Evidential Methods

We reanalyzed both ARDS trials using an evidential framework, examining VFDs and mortality at the longest follow-up; only mortality was reanalyzed for BaSICS. The technical aspects of the analyses are presented in Table E1 in the data supplement, along with the code. We employed linear regression for VFDs (for ART and STAMINA) and logistic regression for mortality (for all trials), with both analyses being unadjusted. The first step was to define the likelihood function for the continuous and binary endpoints. When these functions had been established, LR and S values for relevant comparisons were calculated (Tables 3 and E2). Sequential analysis of S values over time was also performed (see below).

ART and STAMINA VFD Analysis

Evidential methods enable readers to select the comparisons of greatest interest, such as the relative evidence for a 1-day increase versus a 1-day decrease in VFDs, to assess potential harm. The likelihood functions for VFDs for ART and STAMINA are illustrated in Figure 2, with results summarized in Table 3. For ART, the analysis revealed very low LRs for benefit, resulting in negative S values, which align with fewer VFDs. The S−2 support interval between −2.2 and −0.1 days indicates that S > 2 for the MLE compared with the null in the direction of harm. Evidential methods further show that the intervention’s likelihood for harm is magnified when compared with the possibility of benefit (one additional vs. one fewer VFD), relative to assessing the likelihood of harm versus no effect (one additional VFD vs. no difference in VFDs).

Results for mortality and ventilator-free days for ART and STAMINA. The maximum likelihood estimate is shown on the label, and support−2 and support−3 intervals are presented on the gray bars. (A and C) Likelihood function for the difference in mortality. The maximum likelihood estimator (Table 2) is displayed, representing the absolute difference in mortality observed in each trial. Differences of 2% are indicated by dashed lines (red for increase, blue for decrease). The dashed blue line is nearly invisible because 2% reductions in mortality have a low likelihood. (B and D) Likelihood function for the difference in ventilator-free days for each trial. The dashed lines denote a change of 1 day alive and free of mechanical ventilation (reduction in red, increase in blue).

The STAMINA trial results also favored the control group, although they were less conclusive because of the smaller sample size. Nonetheless, as shown in Table 3, the data provided weak evidence against the hypothesis that the STAMINA strategy increased VFDs compared with a decrease of 1 day (S = −1.7). Support plots are presented in Figure E1.
Mortality Analysis

Clinicians may be interested in specific hypotheses, as outlined in Table 3 (for ART and STAMINA) and Table E2 (for BaSICS). For ART and STAMINA, this includes relative evidence for changes in mortality rate of 2% (which may be considered a feasible minimal clinically important difference and is considerably lower than the difference those trials were powered to detect); other effects were also explored. The likelihood functions appear in Figure 2 (ART and STAMINA) and Figure E2 (BaSICS). For ART, there was moderate evidence for a 2% increase in mortality rate compared with no change and very strong evidence for a 2% increase compared with a 2% decrease. Additionally, there was overwhelming evidence against a 5% decrease compared with a 1% increase (Table 3). STAMINA displayed a similar pattern, albeit less pronounced, with weak evidence for a 2% increase versus a 2% decrease and moderate evidence against a 5% decrease compared with a 1% increase. For BaSICS, the results were compatible with the neutral main trial results, but interesting information was obtained (see Table E2). For example, there was exceedingly strong evidence against a 3.5% mortality reduction (the effect size used for sample size estimation in the trial) versus no effect (S = −9.13). S−2 intervals ranged from a 2% reduction in mortality to a 0.4% increase in mortality. There was very strong evidence for a 1% decrease in mortality versus a 1% increase (S = 4.33). This confirms that a 3.5% mortality reduction is very unlikely with balanced solutions (which aligns with an individual-patient meta-analysis), and that it is much more likely that the intervention decreases mortality by 1% than increases mortality by the same amount.
Support over Time for Trial Monitoring

Monitoring in clinical trials is critical for patient safety and resource optimization. The evidential framework offers a complementary approach to traditional interim (i.e., at specific time points) analyses by allowing direct assessment of evolving evidence with fewer constraints than conventional statistical adjustment procedures (hence the term sequential, meaning that analyses are not fixed to specific time points). This approach shares conceptual similarities with sequential probability ratio tests (SPRTs) pioneered by Wald, though with important distinctions. Classical SPRTs compare LRs against predetermined boundaries to make binary decisions while controlling error rates. However, SPRTs face limitations in complex trial designs with time-varying effects and adaptive features common in modern critical-care trials. The evidential approach we present focuses on continuous evidence assessment, which may be adapted in a way that preserves error rates in certain contexts, as we will see later. For our sequential analysis implementations, we incorporated structured run-in phases with minimum patient enrollments (50 for ART and STAMINA, 250 for BaSICS) before beginning monitoring. These run-in phases ensure sufficient data for stable model convergence and prevent potentially misleading evidence fluctuations that commonly occur with very small sample sizes. Run-in sizes were pragmatically determined based on model complexity and total expected enrollment, with larger trials requiring proportionally larger initial samples.

The ART sample size was event-driven, and interim analyses were planned at approximately 33% and 66% of all enrolled patients using the Haybittle-Peto rule to stop for harm (a P < 0.01 for mortality). We plot the support for conceivable hypotheses over time for mortality (Figure 3A) and VFDs (Figure 3B). Note how strong evidence against possible benefits appeared much earlier in the trial. From a patient safety perspective, it could be justified that the trial should have been stopped earlier when sustained strong evidence against benefit emerged. For ART, support for any benefit became sharply less likely at approximately 750 patients. This could reflect, for example, a change in case mix (which would signal potential heterogeneity in treatment effect) or a change in enrollment site mix (which could suggest effect heterogeneity at the site level, such as new sites being less experienced with the maneuver). For STAMINA, results were less pronounced, especially regarding mortality. However, support against an increase in VFDs (vs. a decrease) became pronounced and steadily increased after the first 100 patients, with moderate evidence sustained at approximately 160 patients. This suggests that, even if the trial had proceeded after its early termination, the results would likely indicate harm. In BaSICS (Figure 4), support for the predetermined effect size (3.5% reduction) was already low at 3,000 patients, and support for other effect sizes remained constant after 8,000 patients. This information could have potentially guided trial execution or termination.

To evaluate the statistical properties of likelihood-based monitoring, we conducted extensive simulation studies comparing conventional and likelihood-based stopping rules. These simulations, detailed in Figures E3 and E4 and Tables E3–E5, demonstrate that likelihood-based monitoring can feasibly control type I error and power. However, an important caveat remains: the precise relationship between LR thresholds and conventional error rates is not straightforward. Unlike traditional monitoring boundaries, LR-based stopping rules do not directly correspond to specific type I error probabilities without additional calibration. Trial-specific simulations would be needed to establish LR thresholds that achieve the desired error control properties, an important consideration for formal implementation that warrants further methodological research (see Figures E3 and E4 and Tables E3–E5).
Recommendations for Conducting and Reporting an Evidential Analysis

To facilitate the adoption of evidential methods in clinical research, we propose standardized reporting formats that enhance clarity while remaining compatible with existing conventions. In methods sections, authors should explicitly define: 1) the likelihood function used for analysis, 2) the specific parameter of interest and its clinical significance, 3) prespecified LR thresholds for interpretation, and 4) the rationale for selected hypothesis comparisons. Visualizations should display likelihood functions with clearly marked MLEs, S−2 and S−3 intervals, and vertical reference lines indicating clinically relevant effect sizes (as in Figure 2).

When presented alongside frequentist (and, if appropriate, Bayesian) metrics, authors should report evidential findings in parallel with conventional measures, including contextualization. For example, one possible way to present the results of ART could be: “The ART trial showed a 6.0% absolute increase in mortality in the intervention group compared with the control (55.3% vs. 49.3%; P = 0.041), indicating that, if the null hypothesis of no effect were true, we would observe a treatment effect of this magnitude or greater in approximately 4% of similar trials. The evidential analysis provides moderate evidence favoring a 2% increase in mortality over no effect (LR = 7.35; S = 2.0) and very strong evidence favoring a 2% increase over a 2% decrease in mortality (LR = 120.94, S = 4.8). A complementary Bayesian analysis using a moderately informative skeptical prior (log[odds ratio] ≈ N[0,0.355]) yields a posterior odds ratio of 1.24 (95% credible interval, 0.98–1.56), with a 96.3% probability of increased mortality with the intervention and only a 0.7% probability that the intervention reduces mortality by ≥2%.” Taken together, these results suggest that the intervention was probably harmful in ART. The evidential approach confirms that significant harm is much more likely than significant benefit, independent of prior belief. The Bayesian analysis with zero-centered priors that are skeptical of large effect sizes inferred the probability of a relevant benefit to be <0.7%. This integrated reporting approach contextualizes likelihood-based evidence within familiar frameworks while highlighting the unique insights provided by comparative evidential assessment.
Discussion

Evidential methods provide a flexible inferential framework that aligns with clinical reasoning, enabling targeted questions about the relative evidence for competing hypotheses about treatment effects. Unlike Bayesian methods, this approach does not require specification of prior distributions and focuses solely on the relative compatibility of the observed data with different effect sizes, providing a more direct assessment of evidence without combining data with external beliefs. Our reanalyses of the ART, STAMINA, and BaSICS trials demonstrate several ways the evidential framework can augment and enhance the execution and interpretation of critical care trials.

First, evidential methods directly address the clinical question: “How strongly do our data support one meaningful effect over another?” Unlike P values or Bayesian posteriors, LRs enable direct comparison of competing scenarios without statistical adjustment penalties. This is particularly valuable for flexible data interrogation in critical care. For point hypotheses, these LRs are mathematically equivalent to Bayes factors, creating a natural connection to Bayesian inference without requiring priors. Our analyses demonstrate this advantage: ART data showed 121-fold stronger support for a 2% mortality increase versus a 2% decrease, STAMINA data demonstrated 5.3-fold stronger support for the same comparison, and BaSICS confirmed that the hypothesized 3.5% mortality reduction was unlikely while providing evidence for the safety of balanced solutions. This approach has particular relevance for noninferiority analysis by directly quantifying relative evidence for different margins of effect without requiring dichotomous decisions based on P values or posterior probabilities.

Second, S−2 support intervals provide an intuitive measure of uncertainty by conveying ranges of effect sizes reasonably compatible with observed data. Unlike confidence intervals that describe where the true effect might lie across hypothetical repeated experiments, or Bayesian credible intervals that combine data with prior beliefs, S intervals focus solely on how compatible each possible effect size is with the actual data collected. This direct evidence approach aligns with clinical reasoning, identifying which treatment effects remain plausible based on study results without requiring statistical abstractions or external assumptions. The interval width provides straightforward information about evidence precision while maintaining an interpretive framework centered on what the data directly support.

Third, evidential analysis enhances trial safety monitoring. Our sequential analysis of ART demonstrated evidence against meaningful benefits emerging earlier than would be detected through traditional interim analyses. Visual inspection of support over time provides valuable information to data safety monitoring boards, potentially identifying benefit and harm patterns earlier than conventional methods would. Some theoretical work suggests that evidence-based comparisons may maintain certain robustness properties even under model uncertainty, though the full implications of this for clinical trials remain to be explored. Our initial simulation work, although limited, indicates that constrained stopping rules based on evidence strength can maintain acceptable false positive rates. However, the formal statistical properties of evidence-based sequential monitoring schemes require further investigation, particularly regarding error control across different trial contexts and endpoint types.

Fourth, evidential analysis is methodologically agnostic, requiring neither frequentist philosophical commitments nor Bayesian priors, while yielding results interpretable alongside traditional metrics when needed.

It is important to clarify that, although the evidential approach facilitates direct comparisons between benefit and harm scenarios, this should not be misinterpreted as lowering the threshold for accepting interventions with uncertain benefits. The principle of “first, do no harm” remains foundational in critical care medicine, and evidential methods should complement, not replace, careful consideration of net clinical benefit and potential harms. Evidential methods could potentially enhance patient safety by explicitly quantifying the relative evidence for harm versus benefit, as demonstrated in our ART analysis, in which there was overwhelming evidence against clinically meaningful benefit compared with a small risk of harm. This approach aligns with ethical clinical practice by providing transparent evidence assessment while respecting the asymmetric burden of proof appropriately required for interventions: stronger evidence should be required to adopt an intervention than to abandon it when harm is possible.

Limitations include the potential for categorical interpretation of continuous evidence (e.g., S > 2 as “moderate evidence”), which may lead to binary thinking similar to significance testing. Unlike Bayesian methods that offer probabilistic statements about effect sizes, evidential methods focus on the relative plausibility between specific values and cannot provide absolute probabilities for hypotheses. Although Bayesian analyses with minimally informative priors produce numerically similar results, the evidential approach offers a philosophically distinct framework that may appeal to researchers who prefer to avoid any prior specification or who find the direct comparison of data compatibility more intuitive than probabilistic statements about hypotheses. This means that evidential methods cannot directly answer questions like “What is the probability that this treatment reduces mortality by at least X%?” Furthermore, there is no clear consensus on LR or S thresholds for decision-making in clinical research, which can result in inconsistent application. We encourage viewing support values on a continuous spectrum and considering multiple competing hypotheses rather than focusing on single binary comparisons.

Additionally, although evidential methods for simple models are well established, approaches for complex analyses, such as time-to-event outcomes, clustered data, multiple covariates, and competing risk models, remain less developed, with limited software available. The likelihoodR package and our online Shiny app (https://fzampier.shinyapps.io/Likelihood_Shiny/) facilitate implementation. However, guidance on sample size calculation and sequential analyses using solely evidential approaches remains limited.

Finally, it is important to acknowledge that frequentist, Bayesian, and evidential approaches ultimately represent different philosophical lenses for examining the same data, and each has merit depending on the goals of an analysis. In many situations, these approaches converge numerically: confidence intervals, Bayesian credible intervals with weak priors, and S−2 support intervals often yield similar ranges; P values can be transformed into minimum Bayes factors; and LRs equal Bayes factors for point hypotheses. The choice between approaches often reflects the investigator’s philosophical stance, communication goals, and practical constraints rather than fundamental statistical superiority. The evidential framework may offer value when investigators seek direct comparisons between competing hypotheses without committing to sampling distributions or prior specifications. Rather than viewing these as competing paradigms, we suggest they form a complementary toolkit, with the optimal choice depending on the specific research question, audience, and decision-making context.
Conclusions

The evidential framework represents an alternative method of statistical inference in clinical research that occupies a middle ground between frequentist and Bayesian paradigms. This approach focuses on the relative evidence between competing hypotheses rather than on null hypothesis testing or posterior probabilities. We provided a summary of the main tenets of evidential analysis, LRs for quantifying relative evidence between hypotheses, support values (log-transformed ratios), and S intervals to capture the ranges of plausible effects, along with reporting recommendations. The approach offers complementary insights for understanding trials, particularly for clinicians who find LRs accessible for comparing efficacy and for sequential and interim trial monitoring. Future methodological work is needed to standardize evidential approaches across more complex trial settings and to establish consensus around interpretation thresholds.
